Initial states and a terminal career value#

At the date a customer technology changes, the economy inherits its qualified people and its research frontier, while the private value of a qualification reflects the future wages available from that date onward. Closing a finite career horizon requires a terminal payoff Δ‾\overline\DeltaΔ supplied by a continuation occupation, giving two initial conditions for the physical states and one terminal condition for the forward value.

Given a trial qualification-value path, we can integrate population and frontier forward while clearing the labor market at each date, then integrate the value equation backward from its terminal payoff using the resulting wages. Repeating those updates seeks a path whose physical evolution and anticipated earnings agree, the same logical construction used in the paper’s finite-horizon existence proof.

Within a compact feasible region, uniformly decreasing service demand gives regular wage roots, bounded wages keep private values bounded, and a sufficiently short horizon limits the feedback between the two path updates. Proposition H.1 supplies an explicit contraction condition under which the boundary problem has one equilibrium inside that region, including endogenous changes in the active research allocation.

Local links and complete paths#

Through the shared market, more expertise lowers the human research wage, while greater customer demand raises it, and both price effects change the packets purchased by a fixed fund. At a common frontier in a strict human regime, differentiating clearing gives the displayed local relationship, where dDS∣wdD_S|_wdDS​∣w​ includes customer and qualification-value effects evaluated at the original wage.

Within the feedback graph, Loops follows the connected economic channels, while Strength examines their exact conditional derivatives at the selected state. For positive quantities uuu and vvv, the elasticity (u/v) ∂v/∂u(u/v)\,\partial v/\partial u(u/v)∂v/∂u expresses a local percentage response under the displayed conditioning, while derivatives of accumulation or value equations retain the meaning of their specified flows.

With Shock, changing the customer or research environment recomputes a complete boundary-value path, so future practice, study, headcount, wages, and frontier productivity respond together. Those paths combine the local channels through the career equations and market clearing, allowing a positive link from expertise to research to coexist with a transition whose outcome also reflects released service hours and a different research regime.

Human, mixed, and autonomous allocations have different derivative structures because an interior mixture and an autonomous corner price completed output through the machine cost. At a fixed frontier in those regions, FE=0F_E=0FE​=0, while human research has FE/F=1/(hJ)>0F_E/F=1/(h\mathcal J)>0FE​/F=1/(hJ)>0, and the graph’s selected regime identifies which relationship applies.

When the model retains a human grounding requirement inside the machine route, expertise again changes research output at the grounded corner through the price of that required labor. Equal-cost mixing can still adjust the human share while preserving output per unit of budget, so the complete allocation rule determines which feedback is active.

Why expectations work backward#

Subtracting two private value equations produces a scalar linear equation for their difference, because the difference of squared values factors into their sum times their difference. Backward integration then gives the positive kernel above, whose weight combines ordinary discounting, qualification obsolescence, and the optimized study terms of the two paths.

With common terminal values, every future wage difference enters present qualification value with positive weight, so a lower future wage path lowers today’s study incentive. For bounded global value paths, the terminal term vanishes as the horizon grows, and the same comparison becomes an integral over the entire future, as proved in Proposition G.3.

For an announced machine improvement, the wage difference comes from the endogenous research allocation and its frontier path, with the mixed-regime theorem giving a signed joint example under the relative-productivity condition. Through the kernel, future wage changes that differ in sign contribute according to their place along the full discounted path when determining current investment.

How a numerical path is selected#

At a fixed frontier, the stationary career system has one stable direction and one unstable direction under the strict diagnostic-portfolio conditions, so a nearby inherited expert population selects one locally convergent initial qualification value. Numerical selection can use forward and backward relaxation or vary the initial value until the terminal payoff is satisfied, with feasibility, clearing, and boundary residuals evaluated on the resulting path.

For a longer finite horizon, the shooting residual S(Δ0)=Δ(T)−Ψ(E(T),A(T))S(\Delta_0)=\Delta(T)-\Psi(E(T),A(T))S(Δ0​)=Δ(T)−Ψ(E(T),A(T)) gives a local selection test, since a nonzero derivative S′(Δ0)S'(\Delta_0)S′(Δ0​) allows the implicit-function theorem to identify one nearby initial value. Endogenous equal-cost boundaries preserve the wage level and use piecewise derivatives, while a discrete first-availability event also changes its date under perturbation.

Displayed interactive paths use a specified illustrative economy with positive-premium feasibility and an explicit continuation payoff, and numerical diagnostics describe that selected boundary solution. Once the career mechanism and research allocation are linked, frontier growth follows from their long-run production requirements and from the time needed to put new research capability to work.
